segments.text: Joining me is V. Anant Nageswaran, Chief Economic Advisor to Government of India.
segments.speaker: SPEAKER_01

segments.text: Sir, welcome.
segments.speaker: SPEAKER_01

segments.text: You work closely with the Prime Minister.
segments.speaker: SPEAKER_01

segments.text: You're a part of this journey, Viksit Bharat, by 2047.
segments.speaker: SPEAKER_01

segments.text: As India emerges as the fastest growing major economy, in your view, sir, how much of this is the reforms he initiated?
segments.speaker: SPEAKER_01

segments.text: What do you make of this journey so far?
segments.speaker: SPEAKER_01

segments.text: Thank you for having me on your show and it's a, I mean, to answer your question, I would say a very, very high proportion of the credit to India's journey towards becoming a Vixit Bharat and the fact that many Indians are even able to
segments.speaker: SPEAKER_00

segments.text: aspire for and dream of that possibility owes a lot to the kind of economic stewardship that the honorable prime minister has provided in the last 12 years.
segments.speaker: SPEAKER_00

segments.text: He inherited an economy that was partly or largely broken because we had a high current account deficit.
segments.speaker: SPEAKER_00

segments.text: We had double-digit inflation rates, and we had a currency that had just cratered, and fiscal deficit was very high, and the banking system was in a crisis, and so were corporate balance sheets.
segments.speaker: SPEAKER_00

segments.text: We should not forget that these were the legacy that he inherited on the macroeconomic front.
segments.speaker: SPEAKER_00

segments.text: So, given that, to have repaired the bank balance sheets, and today, Indian banks not performing assets are at a historical low, and the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code also helped corporate balance sheets to become healthy, and then he unleashed financial inclusion to the PM Jandan Yojana,
segments.speaker: SPEAKER_00

segments.text: and then handled COVID so well compared to many other nations that India was able to recover and bounce back with very high growth rates in 2021-22 and 2022-23 and sustain them in the following three years as well.
segments.speaker: SPEAKER_00

segments.text: And I'm leaving out an important landmark reform, single nation, single tax, the goods and services tax, apart from the fact that from 2017-18,
segments.speaker: SPEAKER_00

segments.text: Public investment in infrastructure and capital expenditure had gone up by three and a half to four x four times.
segments.speaker: SPEAKER_00

segments.text: And so much so that India's infrastructure when it comes to airports, road connectivity, energy generation, the number of metro cities that have metro rail and the inland water transport for free, etc.
segments.speaker: SPEAKER_00

segments.text: If you really look at them, these have lifted India's potential growth rate.
segments.speaker: SPEAKER_00

segments.text: And it also lifted India's aspirations and all the while maintaining macroeconomic stability, having inherited a very high fiscal deficit.
segments.speaker: SPEAKER_00

segments.text: And with the COVID compounding it, he has fixed it.
segments.speaker: SPEAKER_00

segments.text: India earned its first credit rating upgrade in 2025.
segments.speaker: SPEAKER_00

segments.text: So we can go on.
segments.speaker: SPEAKER_00

segments.text: So clearly it's interesting you point out sir that from fragile five he was in 2013-14 he's been able to bring it to the fastest growing large economy right now but the challenges you know that were en route and we'll talk about those in a moment but the challenges right now
segments.speaker: SPEAKER_01

segments.text: There are many who say jobs for example, or private investment for example, that's yet to pick up at the full scale.
segments.speaker: SPEAKER_01

segments.text: In your view sir, what's holding that back?
segments.speaker: SPEAKER_01

segments.text: What more needs to be done to unlock that animal instinct or that potential?
segments.speaker: SPEAKER_01

segments.text: No, you are right.
segments.speaker: SPEAKER_00

segments.text: The private corporate sector, but first of all, let me tell you that India's overall capital formation rate at 33%, 34% of GDP is a very high number.
segments.speaker: SPEAKER_00

segments.text: So there is capital formation happening.
segments.speaker: SPEAKER_00

segments.text: And you can say that it is because of public investment by government and the state governments as well, given the 50-year interest-free loans.
segments.speaker: SPEAKER_00

segments.text: And within the private sector, I think there are some research reports that show that
segments.speaker: SPEAKER_00

segments.text: listed companies have been doing better than non-listed companies or unlisted companies when it comes to capital formation.
segments.speaker: SPEAKER_00

segments.text: But the biggest reason that you are looking at a much higher number, but it is not there, are multiple.
segments.speaker: SPEAKER_00

segments.text: One is the global uncertainty, the extraordinarily high degree of manufacturing competition coming from China, given their own deflation, given their own domestic economy travails,
segments.speaker: SPEAKER_00

segments.text: They rely extremely heavily on exports, and their deflation is making them utilize the global markets, which naturally makes investors in other countries pull back and decide when to put their money to work, et cetera.
segments.speaker: SPEAKER_00

segments.text: But having said that, India's capital formation in the private sector is beginning to rise in the last few quarters.
segments.speaker: SPEAKER_00

segments.text: And the bank credit growth to industry is running at 20 percent.
segments.speaker: SPEAKER_00

segments.text: And I think given the kind of steady growth rate that we have witnessed in the Indian economy, the private sector capital formation and I hear I refer to the unlisted space.
segments.speaker: SPEAKER_00

segments.text: I think it will catch up with the households and with the public sector, in fact, making them step back a bit.
segments.speaker: SPEAKER_00

segments.text: And private sector capital formation will probably take over the baton from these two segments of the economy.
segments.speaker: SPEAKER_00

segments.text: Back to you.
segments.speaker: SPEAKER_00

segments.text: Sir, you spoke of the global headwinds.
segments.speaker: SPEAKER_01

segments.text: You know, you spoke of COVID-19.
segments.speaker: SPEAKER_01

segments.text: So 2020, that was a huge challenge.
segments.speaker: SPEAKER_01

segments.text: Then 2022, the Russia-Ukraine war, both energy and fertilizers, adversely impacted.
segments.speaker: SPEAKER_01

segments.text: Then again 2025 and 2026, you've had Iran, U.S.
segments.speaker: SPEAKER_01

segments.text: and Israel conflict, the impact again on energy and fertilizers.
segments.speaker: SPEAKER_01

segments.text: What's it like working with the Prime Minister when these challenges come and you sit in the Prime Minister's office and talk about how do you overcome these challenges?
segments.speaker: SPEAKER_01

segments.text: Of course, I mean, I don't sit in the Prime Minister's office.
segments.speaker: SPEAKER_00

segments.text: The Chief Economic Adviser's office is part of the Ministry of Finance, but I do.
segments.speaker: SPEAKER_00

segments.text: do regular periodic updates on the macro situation to the Honorable Prime Minister.
segments.speaker: SPEAKER_00

segments.text: I think one of the things that you alluded to in your own initial intro remarks is his laser-like focus and his ability to remember details and to ensure follow-up and a steady hand, at the same time not losing focus on the underlying inherent strengths of the economy
segments.speaker: SPEAKER_00

segments.text: for meeting short-term needs.
segments.speaker: SPEAKER_00

segments.text: He doesn't sacrifice the long-term macroeconomic stability or financial prudence.
segments.speaker: SPEAKER_00

segments.text: Even if the short-term situation calls for remedies, he's able to keep an eye on the medium-term strings that have been serving Indian economy very well over the last 12 years, even as he has to take short-term measures to make sure that the economy is able to handle the crisis.
segments.speaker: SPEAKER_00

segments.text: We saw that in the pandemic.
segments.speaker: SPEAKER_00

segments.text: We saw that during the 2022 Russia-Ukraine crisis, and even this year in ensuring supply of cooking gas, natural gas, crude oil, diversifying the sources, using the crisis to make people move from cooking gas to pipe, natural gas, et cetera.
segments.speaker: SPEAKER_00

segments.text: And then in the last two years, you have seen the liberalization of nuclear energy.
segments.speaker: SPEAKER_00

segments.text: The draft rules have been announced recently and also launching
segments.speaker: SPEAKER_00

segments.text: the critical minerals and earth's mission.
segments.speaker: SPEAKER_00

segments.text: So it is the ability to manage the short-term crisis and the exigency while keeping a very firm and clear-eyed focus on the medium to long-term priorities, I would say, are his core strengths.
segments.speaker: SPEAKER_00

segments.text: Okay and you know you've talked of GDP growth numbers they remain strong 7.8 percent even though there was a storm in a teacup or more politically over certain numbers but if we were to come to rural income for example or wages you know which would give you that sense that
segments.speaker: SPEAKER_01

segments.text: as India grows that journey towards Viksit Bharat, salaries are also going up.
segments.speaker: SPEAKER_01

segments.text: Now, that also remains under pressure.
segments.speaker: SPEAKER_01

segments.text: Now, what more needs to be done and what is the Prime Minister and your entire team, you know, the finance minister, you, the entire team doing to ensure that the growth should be felt across sectors.
segments.speaker: SPEAKER_01

segments.text: Yeah, absolutely, undoubtedly.
segments.speaker: SPEAKER_00

segments.text: I mean, economic growth per se would count for very little unless it touches people's lives and makes a difference.
segments.speaker: SPEAKER_00

segments.text: There should be no doubt about that.
segments.speaker: SPEAKER_00

segments.text: And rural income and rural employment growth, if you look at the annual numbers, they have been steadily improving post-COVID.
segments.speaker: SPEAKER_00

segments.text: In fact, it is the recent monthly data that have been somewhat cyclically
segments.speaker: SPEAKER_00

segments.text: Drifting lower but annual numbers show a very robust growth in both the rural employment and incomes clearly rural income growth the cyclical in nature and this year's monsoon has introduced a certain sense of uncertainty.
segments.speaker: SPEAKER_00

segments.text: with respect to agricultural output and rural demand down the road, so government will be very much alive to the situation and responding to that if necessary.
segments.speaker: SPEAKER_00

segments.text: But to your broader question about what we should be doing, and in fact the government has been doing a lot, I think memories are a bit short these days because of the onslaught of information from social media.
segments.speaker: SPEAKER_00

segments.text: But July 2024 budget by the government was exclusively focused on employment, whether it is corporate internship, apprenticeship schemes, incentives for first-time jobs created by companies in manufacturing and in non-manufacturing sectors, contributing to some of the provident fund contributions by the employees, the government taking over the employer's contribution so that
segments.speaker: SPEAKER_00

segments.text: They don't feel disincentivized to hire because of pension contributions which the government took over.
segments.speaker: SPEAKER_00

segments.text: So the entire July 2024 budget was about employment generation.
segments.speaker: SPEAKER_00

segments.text: Second, the labor intensive free trade agreements that the government is now signing
segments.speaker: SPEAKER_00

segments.text: With the UK, it is now active and with the European Union, it is going to become active by the end of the year.
segments.speaker: SPEAKER_00

segments.text: And these agreements open labor intensive goods and services sectors for Indian producers and entrepreneurs.
segments.speaker: SPEAKER_00

segments.text: The third thing that the government is doing, it is actively facilitating deregulation efforts in states.
segments.speaker: SPEAKER_00

segments.text: And that is an effort underway both in the union government, of course, that is separate, but in the states as well, where there is a touch point of the local governments with the businesses, small businesses.
segments.speaker: SPEAKER_00

segments.text: And this deregulation will lower the cost of doing business for small and medium businesses in states and therefore contributing to their hiring much more.
segments.speaker: SPEAKER_00

segments.text: So, I would say, fiscal initiatives, free trade agreements deregulation initiatives, and the various incentives given for capital formation by by the state's 50 year interest free loans.
segments.speaker: SPEAKER_00

segments.text: and ensuring that credit availability to MSMEs.
segments.speaker: SPEAKER_00

segments.text: Look at the MSME credit go from the banking sector, it is running at nearly 23 percent.
segments.speaker: SPEAKER_00

segments.text: So all these things and then the various initiatives given for startups and new businesses, etc.
segments.speaker: SPEAKER_00

segments.text: All of these things, given the uncertainties, despite the global uncertainties, all of these things are contributing to keeping up job creation.
segments.speaker: SPEAKER_00

segments.text: I will continue to facilitate job creation in the Indian economy in the coming years.
segments.speaker: SPEAKER_00

segments.text: And manufacturing, that's been one of the key focus areas and key result areas for the Prime Minister.
segments.speaker: SPEAKER_01

segments.text: We've heard him talk about Atman-e-Bharat Bharat, increased manufacturing on ground.
segments.speaker: SPEAKER_01

segments.text: I mean, considering China manufactures so much that it's exporting finished products, on ground, how much of our manufacturing is actually taking off?
segments.speaker: SPEAKER_01

segments.text: What more needs to be done to ensure that our manufacturing is world-class, competitive, and
segments.speaker: SPEAKER_01

segments.text: export-oriented too.
segments.speaker: SPEAKER_01

segments.text: The entire PLI initiative is all about bringing manufacturing to a greater share of gross value addition, GVA, in the economy.
segments.speaker: SPEAKER_00

segments.text: In fact, in constant prices, India's manufacturing share of GVA has been rising from 14 percent something to 16.1 percent in the last three years in constant price terms.
segments.speaker: SPEAKER_00

segments.text: And I think apart from the PLA initiatives ensuring energy availability, ensuring skilling, creating these free trade agreements so that manufacturing can export goods with lower or no duties, etc.
segments.speaker: SPEAKER_00

segments.text: and also reducing the customs duties on intermediate goods and inputs, which were the major plans of the budget announced in February, 2026.
segments.speaker: SPEAKER_00

segments.text: And then creating demand visibility for manufactured goods in the country through reduction in direct taxes and indirect taxes in the course of 2025.
segments.speaker: SPEAKER_00

segments.text: All these are all measures to ensure that Indian businesses
segments.speaker: SPEAKER_00

segments.text: continue to grow their manufacturing share because free trade agreements bring in an element of competition as well and then also induce businesses to invest in R&D.
segments.speaker: SPEAKER_00

segments.text: So multiple measures are underway and the manufacturing share of GVA rising is showing that these efforts are bearing fruit.
segments.speaker: SPEAKER_00

segments.text: And how would you describe you know Prime Minister Narendra Modi's personal role in shaping the economic policies in the past 12 years and of course the road ahead because 4 trillion dollars to reach that 30 trillion dollar mark by 2047 this will have to grow a multi-fold and manifold now sir.
segments.speaker: SPEAKER_01

segments.text: To describe his personal goal is to simply say that he is the architect of the economic policy.
segments.speaker: SPEAKER_00

segments.text: He is the architect of the manufacturing vision and of the world class infrastructure that India has been creating over the last 12 years.
segments.speaker: SPEAKER_00

segments.text: And also, he is the one who anticipated the supply chain disruptions and weaponization that could happen, and which is why he called for Atman-Irbarta and indigenization since the Russia-Ukraine war broke out.
segments.speaker: SPEAKER_00

segments.text: And I think his emphasis on indigenization is turning out to be prescient.
segments.speaker: SPEAKER_00

segments.text: even that more and more supply chain choke points and weaponization is emerging increasingly so in the world.
segments.speaker: SPEAKER_00

segments.text: And then when you look at the fiscal prudence and fiscal stability, which has brought down the overall interest rates in the Indian economy, even though it has gone up in the last few weeks or so, the 10-year bond yield at 7% from India is a historical loss, which is what brought us the
segments.speaker: SPEAKER_00

segments.text: even as it improved the quality of fiscal expenditure by increasing the capital expenditure share and lowering the revenue expenditure share.
segments.speaker: SPEAKER_00

segments.text: All of these things are, he is the architect of all these policies, whether it is financial inclusion, Jandan Yojana and the mobile phone and the Jam Trinity, digital public infrastructure, we all know that
segments.speaker: SPEAKER_00

segments.text: He is a big believer in the role of technology in improving lives and improving efficiency in the economy.
segments.speaker: SPEAKER_00

segments.text: So I would say his imprint is very evident in almost every major policy initiative and the macroeconomic stability that have underpinned India's rise amidst massively rising global uncertainties.
segments.speaker: SPEAKER_00

segments.text: So that is why we are confident that while there are challenges, because we are a lower middle income economy right now, there are challenges.
segments.speaker: SPEAKER_00

segments.text: about in geopolitics, in climate change, in supply chain, et cetera.
segments.speaker: SPEAKER_00

segments.text: We are confident that we can meet these challenges because he has focus, he has determination, and he has vision and the passion to deliver on India's Vixit Bharat aspirations.
segments.speaker: SPEAKER_00

segments.text: Sir, for joining me here on this India First special broadcast because that vision and that dream of a vikasit Bharat by 2047, you know, that's actually a nation's dream to be a developed country and that inclusive development.
segments.speaker: SPEAKER_01

segments.text: Many thanks for joining me and hope to have you on India First more often.
segments.speaker: SPEAKER_01

segments.text: Many thanks, sir.
segments.speaker: SPEAKER_01

segments.text: Welcome.
